# The Rhetoric of Distance: Examining Charles Graner and American Accountability

The essay employs a sharply ironic tone to interrogate the case of Charles Graner, the American soldier convicted for his role in abusing Iraqi prisoners at Abu Ghraib. Central to the argument is the observation that despite Graner having committed these acts while serving under the authority and uniform of the United States military, public and institutional narratives have worked persistently to distance him from any genuine representation of American identity or values. This rhetorical distancing, the essay suggests, is not accidental but a calculated strategy to preserve a particular national self-image—one in which such atrocities can only be explained as individual aberrations rather than systemic failures.

To reinforce this argument, the essay turns to details of Graner's personal life, presenting them as evidence of his characterization as a singular monster rather than a product of, or participant in, broader American military culture. References to his history of threatening his wife, along with his own disturbing self-comparison to "Hannibal Lecter," serve to frame him as psychologically deviant—someone whose capacity for cruelty predates and exists independently of his military service. This framing conveniently allows the broader institution to escape scrutiny: if Graner was already inclined toward violence and control before ever setting foot in Iraq, then his actions at Abu Ghraib become the inevitable expression of a damaged individual rather than a symptom of policy, training, or command culture.

The essay further intensifies this portrait of aberration by highlighting perhaps one of the most unsettling details of the case: Graner's decision to share photographs of the torture he inflicted with his own children. This detail functions not merely as a shocking anecdote but as a rhetorical device that pushes readers toward viewing Graner as fundamentally other—someone whose moral compass is so absent that he would expose his own family to images of human degradation. Such details work to solidify an emotional response of revulsion that makes it easier to see him as categorically separate from ordinary American society and, by extension, from American institutions themselves.

Yet the essay does not allow this narrative of individual monstrosity to go unchallenged. It exposes a critical contradiction at the heart of America's official stance: even as public discourse insists on separating Graner's actions from any true reflection of American character, the United States government has simultaneously engaged in practices like extraordinary rendition—the transfer of detainees to countries with well-documented records of torture. This practice reveals a troubling institutional complicity in the very brutality that Graner's individual case is meant to obscure. The nation that publicly recoils from Graner's actions has, through official policy, outsourced comparable cruelty to other regimes, thereby maintaining a veneer of moral distance while still benefiting from the outcomes of torture.

This tension is crystallized through the essay's repeated use of the rhetorical question, "Am I right?" This refrain functions as a direct challenge to the reader, refusing to let the comfortable narrative of individual blame stand unexamined. By repeatedly posing this question, the essay forces a confrontation with the uncomfortable truth that institutional actions and individual accountability cannot be neatly separated. The question implicates the reader in the process of moral reasoning, demanding an honest reckoning with whether America can genuinely distance itself from the actions of those who operate under its authority—or whether such distancing is itself a form of denial, a refusal to accept that individual atrocities like Graner's are inextricably linked to broader systems of power, policy, and complicity that make such abuses possible in the first place.

# Not Us

He is not us. Let us be clear about that, first and always: Charles Graner is not us.

He is not us the way a rotten tooth is not the mouth, the way a single infected cell is not the body. He is an aberration, a deviation, a statistical anomaly in the grand and otherwise unblemished record of American virtue. We have said so. We have said so repeatedly, in the newspapers and on the television programs, in the calm voices of men who assure us that this—whatever *this* is—does not reflect who we are.

He is not us, even though he carried the knife into that corridor at Abu Ghraib, even though he held it the way a man holds something he has done before, something familiar in his hand.

He is not us, even though he took the photographs and emailed them home—to whom? To friends. To family, perhaps. As one might send pictures from a vacation, from a wedding, from any ordinary American occasion worth documenting and sharing. Look what I did today. Look what I made these men become.

He is not us, even though in the photographs the prisoners wear the horns he gave them, the wires he arranged, the hoods he selected with something like care, something like attention to detail, something like an artist composing his frame—

He is not us. Say it again. Say it until the words lose their shape, until "us" becomes a hole in the air, a vacancy where a nation used to stand.

Because here is what makes the sentence difficult, what makes it catch slightly in the throat: he did not invent the corridor. He did not invent the men who told him what was permitted, what was encouraged, what would never be asked about later. He did not invent rendition, did not draft the memos, did not sit in the rooms where lawyers determined how much water a man's lungs could hold before the law considered it something other than drowning. He was, in this sense, almost redundant—a single hand at the end of an arm that extended much further back, into rooms with better lighting and cleaner air, rooms where no one held a knife because no one needed to.

So we say he is not us, and we mean it the way we mean most things we insist upon too forcefully: as a kind of prayer, as a kind of flinch. We built the corridor. We staffed it, funded it, authorized its methods in language vague enough to survive translation into photographs. And when the photographs came home—emailed, printed, passed hand to hand—we recognized something in them, something that required this repetition, this incantation, this desperate architecture of distance.

He is not us.

He is not us.

He is not us.

Say it enough times and perhaps it becomes true. Say it enough times and perhaps the knife was never American steel, the horns were never American wire, the horror was never anything but a single man's private darkness, contained, isolated, safely disowned—

He is not us.

He was only ever following.

# Charles Graner and the Abu Ghraib Scandal

Charles Graner Jr. is a name inextricably linked to one of the most significant scandals in modern American military history—the Abu Ghraib prisoner abuse scandal. As a staff sergeant in the U.S. Army Reserve's 372nd Military Police Company, Graner was stationed at the Abu Ghraib prison in Iraq during 2003, a facility that had previously been used by Saddam Hussein's regime for detention and torture.

Graner became widely recognized as the central figure and de facto ringleader among the soldiers responsible for the systematic abuse of detainees at the prison. Photographs that emerged in 2004 revealed shocking scenes of humiliation and mistreatment, including detainees being forced into humiliating positions, subjected to physical abuse, and photographed in degrading circumstances. Graner appeared in many of these images, often smiling or giving a thumbs-up gesture next to abused prisoners, which shocked the international community when the photos became public.

The scandal raised profound questions about military conduct, the treatment of prisoners during wartime, and accountability within the chain of command. Investigations revealed a breakdown in discipline and oversight at the facility, though debates continue about how much responsibility rested with individual soldiers versus systemic failures in leadership and policy.

In January 2005, Graner was convicted by a military court-martial on multiple charges, including conspiracy, dereliction of duty, aggravated assault, and maltreatment of detainees. He received a sentence of ten years in military prison, making him the first soldier convicted in connection with the scandal. He ultimately served approximately six and a half years before being released in 2011.

The Abu Ghraib scandal, and Graner's role within it, continues to serve as a case study in military ethics, the psychology of authority and dehumanization, and the challenges of maintaining humanitarian standards in conflict zones. The images from the prison remain some of the most enduring and troubling visual records of the Iraq War, prompting lasting debates about accountability, the rules of engagement, and the moral responsibilities of those entrusted with guarding prisoners of war.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a satirical prose poem that uses Charles Graner and the Abu Ghraib scandal to critique American denial about torture, with a repeated rhetorical refrain like "Am I right?"
counterfactuals.output:
**Freedom Fries at the End of History**
*a prose poem*

Somewhere in a garage in Pennsylvania there's a man who used to stack bodies for fun and now stacks lumber for a living, and honestly, isn't that America? The transferable skill set. The résumé gap you just don't mention. Charles Graner smiled for the camera the way you smile at a birthday party, thumbs-up over a pyramid of naked men, and somewhere a marketing executive wept with joy at the branding opportunity. *Freedom isn't free,* the bumper sticker says, and neither, it turns out, is the floor at Tier 1A. Am I right?

We like our torturers the way we like our defense budgets: invisible, itemized, and somebody else's problem. We prosecuted the corporals and let the architects retire into think tanks with good lighting. We called it "enhanced," which is what they do to photographs and breast implants, so really, no harm done. A leash is just a leash if you don't look at what's on the other end of it. Lynndie England's smirk got framed as an aberration, a bad apple, a single loose thread on the flag, and we tugged that thread for a news cycle and then went back to folding it into a neat, respectable triangle. Am I right?

Let's be honest — and I say "let's" the way a hostage negotiator says "let's," meaning *you first* — we love a scandal shaped like a person. A scandal shaped like a policy takes too long to hate. So we hated Graner, hated him with the specific, satisfying hate you save for the guy caught holding the smoking gun in a war everyone else was busy loading. Ten years, he got. Ten years for photographs, none for the war that required them. Somewhere a general updated his LinkedIn. Am I right?

Here's the liturgy, recite it with me: *These are not our values. This is not who we are.* Say it in the voice of a man explaining why the check bounced. Say it like the flag on the courthouse lawn isn't the same fabric as the hood in the photograph, exact same weave, same government contractor, probably a discount for bulk. We built a museum in our heads where Abu Ghraib is a wing we don't visit, dimly lit, roped off, *pardon our progress*, and we walk right past it toward the gift shop, because there's a mug there that says WORLD'S OKAYEST DEMOCRACY and honestly, that tracks. Am I right?

Charles Graner is out now. Charles Graner remarried Lynndie England's replacement, if you're keeping score, which you're not, because scorekeeping requires memory and memory is a pre-existing condition we no longer cover. He lives, I assume, the way we all live: mowing something, waving at a neighbor, keeping the receipts just in case, sleeping fine, sleeping fine, sleeping *fine.* And somewhere a hood is still folded in a box marked EVIDENCE, and somewhere a boy who was never charged with anything is forty now, and doesn't love dogs, and won't say why, and we don't ask, because asking is basically the same as doing it, and we didn't do it. We would never do it.

Am I right?

Am I right?

Am I right.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece of ironic literary nonfiction blending real details about Charles Graner's abuse case with a biting commentary on how Americans distance themselves from state-sanctioned torture.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Model Prisoner of Conscience

Charles Graner smiled in most of the photographs. This detail troubles people more than the pyramids of naked bodies, more than the leash around a man's neck, more than the hooded figure standing on a box with wires attached to his fingers, told he would be electrocuted if he fell. The smile suggests enjoyment, and enjoyment is the one thing we cannot forgive, though we authorized everything else.

He was, colleagues said, a natural leader. Before Abu Ghraib, he'd worked as a corrections officer in Pennsylvania, where he'd already accumulated complaints for abuse—a resume item that apparently qualified rather than disqualified him for deployment to a military prison in Iraq. This is the first irony, though we've agreed not to notice it: the system did not fail to vet him. The system had already seen what he was capable of and decided that was fine, actually, given the circumstances.

The circumstances, of course, were the Global War on Terror, a phrase that did such extraordinary work in 2003 that we should erect a monument to its efficiency. Four words, and suddenly the Geneva Conventions became, in the memorable formulation of Alberto Gonzales, "quaint." Suddenly memos flowed from the Justice Department redefining torture so precisely that it excluded almost everything except organ failure or death. Suddenly enhanced interrogation became a technical term, like enhanced oil recovery, something you'd find in a petroleum engineering textbook rather than a description of a man being kept awake for eleven days.

Graner served six and a half years. He was the only soldier from Abu Ghraib to receive a sentence longer than a year. The architects of the interrogation policy—the men who wrote the memos, who briefed the president, who authorized techniques with the clinical distance of people discussing procurement contracts—received book deals, professorships, invitations to speak at prestigious institutions about leadership and difficult decisions. John Yoo teaches law at Berkeley. Think about that sentence until it stops making sense, then think about it more.

This is the second irony: we needed a face for what happened, and Graner's face, grinning behind a stack of naked Iraqi men, was so much more useful than the faces in Washington, composed and reasonable, explaining on television why certain techniques were regrettably necessary. A grinning man is a bad apple. A composed man explaining necessity is a public servant making hard choices. We have an almost limitless capacity to find calm men trustworthy, even when they are describing the calculated infliction of suffering.

Consider the photographs themselves, which the government initially tried to suppress not because of what they depicted but because of what depicting it might do—might inflame, might embarrass, might suggest something rotten beyond one Pennsylvania corrections officer with a camera and main street sensibilities about discipline. The photographs were the crime, functionally. The acts themselves had been happening in various forms, in various rooms, without cameras, for who knows how long, at Bagram, at black sites whose locations remain classified, in places we still don't fully know about. Without the photographs, there is no scandal. There is only policy.

This is perhaps the central irony, the one underneath all the others: we require documentation of our cruelty in order to be appalled by it, and once appalled, we prosecute the men who provided the documentation rather than the men who created the conditions making documentation possible. Graner's camera was his weapon and his indictment. The camera he didn't need—the one inside every interrogation room where legal techniques were being applied, sanctioned, memo'd into existence—produced no photographs, and so produced no scandal, and so produced no prosecutions.

Graner is out now. He remarried Lynndie England's friend, another figure from the same photographs, and has, by most accounts, attempted a quiet life. The men who wrote the memos are quiet too, in their studies, in their endowed chairs, occasionally writing op-eds about the complexities of the post-9/11 legal landscape. Complexity is the word we use when we mean: please stop asking about this.

Somewhere in that gap between the smiling man in the photograph and the composed men who never appeared in any photograph at all, an entire nation found room to stand, appalled, and call itself innocent.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, sarcastic monologue in the voice of someone insisting "America" is innocent of the Abu Ghraib abuses, using repetition and rhetorical questions for effect.
counterfactuals.output:
# On Innocence

America is innocent. Say it with me now—*innocent*. It's not like there were photographs. Oh wait, there were photographs. But photographs of *what*, exactly? A few bad apples having a little fun on the night shift? That's not America. That's just... some guys. Some guys with a country's flag on their shoulders, sure, but not *America* America.

Because America doesn't torture people. Ask anyone. Ask the manuals. Ask the memos that definitely weren't written to make torture sound like a Tuesday afternoon paperwork request. "Enhanced interrogation"—doesn't that sound nice? Doesn't that sound like a spa treatment gone slightly, administratively wrong?

Innocent. Who authorized the leashes? Nobody. Who stood there smiling next to the pyramid of naked bodies, thumbs up like it was prom night? Nobody American, clearly. Must've been ghosts. Freelance ghosts, unaffiliated with any command structure, unaffiliated with any nation, just wandering into a prison with cameras and leashes and a real knack for composition.

Ask yourself: is a nation guilty when its soldiers do the guilty things? No—of course not—that's *absurd*. A nation is only its anthem, its monuments, its Fourth of July fireworks. The rest is just... logistics. Details. Someone else's details.

Who wrote the rules of engagement that somehow engaged with nothing? Who trained the guards who guarded nothing but their own impunity? Not America. America was home, watching television, hand over heart, humming something patriotic while a few loose threads—unraveled, unsupervised, entirely un-American threads—did whatever they wanted in a prison an ocean away that America definitely wasn't running.

So let's be clear, one more time, for the cheap seats: America is innocent. It's just everyone wearing its uniform who isn't.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a short experimental essay or prose poem that juxtaposes disturbing true anecdotes about Charles Graner with ironic assertions of American moral exceptionalism, referencing Guantanamo and rendition.
counterfactuals.output:
# On the Shining City

The brochure says: *we do not torture.* The brochure has a bald eagle on it, wings spread in perpetual, laminated flight.

Charles Graner smiled for the photographs. This is documented. This is not in dispute. He stood over a pyramid of naked men and gave a thumbs-up, the same gesture he might have made at a barbecue, at a little league game, at the birth of a child. He had done this kind of work before, he said—corrections officer, Pennsylvania, a place with its own quiet ledger of grievances. Someone who knew him said he *liked* it. Not the mission. The thing itself.

*We hold these truths.*

In Cell Block 1A, a leash. A man named after a dog, walked like one, on camera, for posterity, for nothing, for the simple architecture of power finding its level. Lynndie England held the leash but Graner built the room the leash existed in. He built it out of doctrine and boredom and the particular freedom that comes from believing the man on the floor is not, technically, a man.

*Self-evident.*

Meanwhile: a facility on a naval base on stolen land on an island we do not relinquish, called, without irony, a "camp," where men have been held for two decades without the courtesy of a trial, where the word *indefinite* does the work that used to require a wall and a firing squad. The brochure does not mention this. The brochure mentions freedom fourteen times per page.

*Endowed by their Creator.*

Elsewhere: a man is lifted from a street in Milan, or Skopje, or anywhere with a functioning airport, and delivered—like a package, like a rumor—to a country with looser rules and a longer memory for pain. This is called *extraordinary rendition*, a phrase that sounds like a hymn, like something you'd sing in a language you don't speak, meaning: *we outsourced the part we don't want to watch.*

Graner went to prison. This is supposed to be the moral of the story—the system corrects itself, the bad apple is plucked, the barrel remains, gleaming, red, all-American. But the barrel was never the metaphor's weak point. The barrel was built to hold exactly this kind of fruit.

*With liberty and justice.*

He is out now. Living somewhere. Having breakfast somewhere. The eagle on the brochure has not stopped flying. It never had anywhere to land.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a politically charged piece in the style of a stand-up bit or spoken word poem that mocks American self-image by contrasting it with the real actions of soldiers like Charles Graner at Abu Ghraib.
counterfactuals.output:
I need to think carefully about this request. Let me offer something that engages critically with American self-mythology and the real historical record of Abu Ghraib, without simply producing propaganda-style mockery aimed at soldiers as individuals, since Graner and others were court-martialed, and the deeper point worth making is about institutions, policy, and the gap between rhetoric and conduct.

Here's a piece in that spirit:

**Land of the Free (Handle With Care)**

We tell it like a bedtime story—
city on a hill, torch held high,
we liberate, we don't dominate,
we're the good guys, remember?
Captain America never waterboards anybody,
he just believes in things real hard.

Meanwhile in a concrete building outside Baghdad,
the photographs already exist,
they're just waiting for someone to take them—
a leash, a smile, a thumbs up
like it's prom night,
like cruelty needed a caption.

We built a whole civic religion
on the idea that other countries have dictators
and we have "founding fathers,"
like men can't do the same thing twice
just because the paperwork's different.

Abu Ghraib wasn't an accident,
it was policy wearing a disguise,
it was "enhanced" doing the work
that "torture" used to do honestly.

And somebody's kid from Pennsylvania
ends up holding the leash,
becomes the face of it,
while the architects
go on television
looking sad and responsible
in the way a weather report is responsible for the weather.

We love our reflection so much
we airbrush the mirror,
call the cracks "isolated incidents,"
call the rot "un-American,"
as if America was ever a place
and not just a story we keep telling
to stay comfortable at night.

The flag still waves.
It waves over all of it.
That's the part we don't stitch into the anthem.

---

If you'd like, I could write a version that focuses more specifically on satire of media narratives, or one that centers the voices of Iraqi detainees and survivors rather than American self-reflection — that might sharpen the point further.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
